newsitem.title: GERMANY: Economists see no Bundesbank rate cut in 97 - poll. [CORRECTED 16:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Economists see no Bundesbank rate cut in 97 - poll. [CORRECTED 16:20 GMT]

text.p: Chances of the Bundesbank cutting leading German interest rates in 1997 are slim, economists polled by Reuters on Tuesday said unanimously.

Any lingering expectations of a rate cut were further dampened on Tuesday by comments by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, quoted in a newspaper interview as saying he saw no need for a cut in German rates for the time being.

Ten German and non-German economists polled by Reuters said they do not expect the Bundesbank to cut its leading interest rates this week, and nine said they do not expect a further cut in the discount and lombard rates this year to help stimulate the economy during the year.
(Corrects number of economists who do not expect the Bundesbank to cut discount and Lombard rates)
The German discount rate currently stands at 2.50 percent and the Lombard emergency financing rate at 4.50 percent. The central bank's main money market rate, the repo, stands at three percent.
The Bundesbank last cut its discount and Lombard rates in April last year and cut the repo rate to three percent in October.
The analysts also said that they thought there would be another fixed repo tender at 3.00 percent at the Bundesbank's first council meeting of 1997 on Thursday.

"The Bundesbank is sending this message -- we will not change medium-term and long-term rates for as long as possible, so as not to unsettle capital markets," said Norbert Meissner, economist at Caisse de Depots Consignations.

From most commentators' point of view, the current economic situation does not require any easing of rates. The improved health of the German exporting and manufacturing sectors are seen to point to an improvement in the overall economy.

While the deutschemark has been higher against the dollar, and is currently at 1994 levels, it has managed to follow a stable course on the currency markets, so currency policy does not require a rate change, analysts said.
Tietmeyer helped keep expectations of a rate cut to a minimum with comments that he saw no need for a change in interest policy for the time being.
He added that the current level of interest rates provided the preconditions for an economic upturn and said that inflation would remain low in 1997.
One possible blot on the horizon, said Klaus Baader of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, is unemployment, which hit record levels of a seasonally-adjusted 4.1 million in November.
However, Baader points out that this is a lagging indicator and an interest rate cut would have no effect on jobs.

Ulrich Beckmann at Deutsche Bank said: "The situation regarding stability is on course, wage increases are under control and domestic prices are also on course. The Bundesbank has no need to react with a rate cut, because the rate of inflation is also not on the way up."
"For full-year 1997 we are looking at a strong level of consistency in the German economic situation," said Beckmann.
Opinions were divided on a possible cut in the closely-watched repo rate, though none expected a cut at next Thursday's meeting.
"We expect the repo rate to be cut within the first quarter of 97 around about ten to 20 basis points -- but not this Thursday," said Keith Edmonds at IBJ International.

Nikolaus Keis at Bayerische Vereinsbank in Munich, said: "If the economy begins to falter, or if the deutschemark begins to weaken, then there is possibly room to manoeuvre on the repo rate of 25 to 30 points downwards."
